Wow, this is news to me!  Since the main thing you're talking about isn't actually defined by HTML, let's discuss over in https://github.com/w3c/pointerevents/issues/177.  Once we figure that out, let's come back to the `click` behavior defined by HTML - maybe we can eliminate that oddity too?

Note that the issue description here is not quite right about what the "firefox behavior" is or the other browsers' behavior, afaict.  See https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-html/2015Oct/0010.html

It looks like Gecko basically stops preventing the dispatching of *all* events on disabled form controls while WebKit and Blink seem to simply ignore event listeners on disabled form controls.

See https://gist.github.com/rniwa/bf0f1411d6b811fcb605e796498740f3

Gecko yields nothing while WebKit and Blink yields:
```
click on div
test on button
test on div
```

I updated my test case a bit (updated the gist). It looks like Gecko is simply truncating the event path at the first disabled form control. This behavior is saner than WebKit/Blink's.

I do have a mild concern that preventing all events from being dispatched on a disabled form control might be a breaking change for some websites. Given WebKit/Blink only has this quirk for `MouseEvent`, that might be good enough.

I'd also add that while WebKit/Blink behavior is very odd, it probably has the least effect to the rest of the event dispatching behavior so it might be something to consider.

Blink has since changed behaviour for mouse events. http://output.jsbin.com/botohet/quiet - the listener here is on the window object (capturing phase). You get mouse/down/up events on the disabled button in Blink, whereas you don't in WebKit.

It's 2019. With https://jsbin.com/cafidayeri/1/edit?html,js,console,output, Firefox seems to allow any synthetic events to be fired on the element itself, except `click` events coming from the browser – precisely the spec behavior. On the other hand, Chrome prevents any `MouseEvent` from firing on the element itself. This includes not just `click` events, but also `mousemove` events, either synthetic or coming from the browser.

Both browsers prevent `click()` from doing anything if a button is disabled.

Relevant WPT: https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/master/html/semantics/forms/attributes-common-to-form-controls/disabled-elements-01.html. This checks that synthetic non-`MouseEvent` event goes through, which seems to be just about the only thing the two browsers agree on.

kind | click `MouseEvent` | mousemove `MouseEvent` | click `Event` | mousemove `Event` | `click()`
---|---|---|---|---|---
synthetic | Chrome no, FF yes, spec yes | Chrome no, FF yes, spec yes | Chrome yes, FF yes, spec ambiguous-to-yes\*; WPT-tested | all yes | all no
natural | all no | Chrome no, FF yes, spec yes

\*: spec says “`click` events”; it’s unclear whether this involves checking if the event is an `MouseEvent` object or not, though I’m inclined to say yes it does as that’s what Chrome and FF agree on.

I want to share a case related to focus events. 

If you have a non-focusable element e.g. `<div />` you can `div.dispatchEvent(new FocusEvent('focus'))` and any focus event listener on the div will be executed. On the  other hand calling `div.focus()` will not dispatch any event.

Dispatching click events on a disabled button will **not** execute click handlers on that button in Chrome. It will also not dispatch click events when calling `button.click()`

A div without a tabIndex acts with regard to focus like a disabled button acts with regard to click.

 IMO I'd prefer to not prevent synthetic events. While this is a somewhat common footgun when writing tests I would always recommend using an imperative method if it exists rather than dispatching synthetic events.

I've been looking at this more recently and I have some new thoughts.

[Jake's article](https://jakearchibald.com/2017/events-and-disabled-form-fields/) and this issue advocate for as many events as possible, including mouseup and mousedown. mousedown and mouseup do seem more problematic since they are similar to the click event and could make a website think that the button is not disabled. I don't know for certain what would happen if we do ship mouseup and mousedown, but I think there is a high risk to websites especially since the UseCounter that @dtapuska added shows [0.11% of page loads](https://chromestatus.com/metrics/feature/timeline/popularity/2321) listening to mouseup and mousedown on disabled form controls, and because no stable browser currently does mouseup or mousedown.

I think that we should allow all events on disabled form controls except mouseup, mousedown, and click.
After getting this done, then we can focus on some more of the edge cases I listed in my previous comment if any are still relevant at that point.

Mousedown is not triggered on disabled elements and NOT even on their parents. The mouse down DOES happen but there's no way for us to react to it, this is a very big deal. This event is responsible for focus loss if something is currently focused and while we can listen to pointerdown which DOES happen – it can also mean that touch scroll action has started and not just a click so it's not a reliable substitute. I filed issues for all browsers:

https://issues.chromium.org/issues/516493667
https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2042317
https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=315556
Can you elaborate why you use mousedown to track focus instead of focus events?

Imagine you have a button with a dropdown. When dropdown is open clicking away or focusing away from the host button should close it. In that dropdown there can be arbitrary content. Clicking that content should not close the dropdown (it's not clicking **away**). If the item inside the dropdown is disabled, clicking it would fire blur event on the host button and there's no way for us to track if we should ignore that blur event because there's no way for us to tell where the mousedown happened that triggered it. For us it looks effectively the same as somebody manually calling button.blur() on our host button which should not keep the dropdown open.

This is just an example off the top of my head. The bottomline is there **was** a mousedown. There were **effects** of that mousedown. We **must** be able to detect that mousedown.
Light dismiss for popovers should still work if you click a disabled button somewhere. Would that be a good enough substitute for your dropdown?

> and there's no way for us to track if we should ignore that blur event because there's no way for us to tell where the mousedown happened that triggered it.

Is [relatedTarget](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/FocusEvent/relatedTarget) not working for this purpose?

No, `relatedTarget` is `null` in both focus going nowhere due to mousedown and manual `blur()` call. Please don't try to come up with workarounds for a particular case. `mousedown` event should definitely trigger on a parent element, how come disabled elements are black hole on the webpage for `mousedown` events? Why `pointerdown` is not affected? Why `pointer-events: none` on disabled elements fixes this? It is just all around **wrong**. I'm performing `mousedown` action on the page – I should be able to detect it.
The reason we are trying to help with other solutions is because this behavior is made for webcompat reason; we can't change it without breaking the web.

I just don't want this discussion to turn into workaround excuses. The case I presented is just a particular situation highlighting that current behavior is wrong, not a sole reason for it to be changed.

Extended the Codepen I used in the issue with all sorts of items that can be disabled:
https://codepen.io/waterplea/pen/qEqPrXb

Inconsistencies with `mousedown` events are (at least in Chrome):
1. Setting `pointer-events: none` actually enabled the `mousedown` event on parent by disabling this event swallowing, which is counter-intuitive to say the least.
2. I can still select input/textarea value with my mouse even if it's disabled meaning selection action of `mousedown` event still works (I thought that's what readonly was for?)
3. `select multiple` gets focused if I click disabled option/optgroup inside of it which means focusing action of `mousedown` event still works
4. Disabled `select multiple` is still scrollable and non-disabled option/optgroup have interaction indication when I click them (absolutely unimportant, of course, just mentioned to illustrate that `mousedown` is happening, just unreachable for the developer)

I get why we might not want to emit `mousedown` event on disabled elements. I would argue we still should since `mouseenter` and `pointerdown` are still emitted and the real event that should be suppressed is `click` event, but I think we can live with that. But why would it swallow event completely and hide it from parent elements? Am I not clicking the page?

If you do not want to change event emitting, then the effects of `mousedown` should also be prevented, as in focus should remain undisturbed if I'm clicking disabled items. As in, if the event is prevented, then it should behave as if preventDefault was called as well,

I do think it's surprising behavior, this is very much related to click being an "activation" event rather than only representing actual click;  a keyboard action can lead to click event on a button for example, as pressing spacebar activates the button. So clicking a disabled button leads to "no activation happened" situation, causing no click event. The reason pointerdown still works but mousedown does not, is that the same logic expanded to mousedown on all browsers (which I don't fully understand why, likely because of legacy pages listening to mousedown on disabled buttons and still expected it to not fire), while pointer events are new and we didn't want to apply the same legacy behavior to those new events.

We could add something like `pointerclick` that does represent only strictly clicks without legacy behavior, but not sure how much push are there for that.
What's your opinion on internally preventing the default of `mousedown` when it happens on a disabled element? This seems like the least intrusive way to make things consistent.
